source.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
source.citation: Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur et al., 2025
source.authors: Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur; E. Lubana; Thomas Fel; Demba E. Ba

record.tranche_reason: Compares SAE architectures using concept-specific F1 scores and latent co-occurrence to test whether unit specialization varies with architecture. It measures SAE latents, not neurons in the underlying networks.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern SAE latents trained on activations, not polysemanticity of the original network's neurons. Results cited from other work are not included as rows. Some reconstruction and sparsity results are not rows because they do not directly measure specialization or polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The paper studies SAE latents, which are units of an interpreter model, not neurons of the networks being interpreted. It assumes base-model neurons are polysemantic as the motivation for SAEs, citing Toy Models and Zoom In. It reports only how specialized the latents of different SAE architectures are, including its own SpaDE. No result measures how often or why the base networks' neurons (DINOv2, the 2-layer GPT) are polysemantic. The architecture comparison is across SAE encoders, not across the base networks' activation functions or architectures, so it does not bear on V5. This is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that each SAE encoder carries implicit assumptions about concept geometry that determine which concepts it can recover. ReLU and JumpReLU assume linear separability; TopK assumes angular separability and uniform dimensionality. No single SAE is universally best. SpaDE, which builds in nonlinear separability and heterogeneity, improves latent specialization in their tests but is not claimed to be optimal.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a theoretical framework for SAE encoder assumptions and compares ReLU, JumpReLU, TopK, and a new SpaDE encoder. It does not reproduce the original neuron visualization or neuron-measurement methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Specialization and latent co-occurrence vary with SAE architecture and, in some experiments, sparsity level. ReLU and JumpReLU cross-concept correlations in the heterogeneity experiment are reported as reduced in the sparse case.

fits_no_version.finding: How monosemantic SAE latents are (F1 score, cross-concept co-occurrence) depends on the SAE encoder architecture. ReLU and JumpReLU fail on nonlinearly separable concepts (F1 at most 0.5). TopK fails to adapt to concepts of different intrinsic dimension. SpaDE reaches F1 of 1.0 in the synthetic and formal-language settings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The monosemanticity of dictionary-learning (SAE) latents depends on whether the encoder's receptive-field assumptions match concept geometry, namely linear separability and uniform intrinsic dimension.

record.problems: The measured units are SAE latents rather than neurons in the base models. The vision experiment uses a 10-class Imagenette subset and 200 latents; the formal-language model is a 2-layer transformer trained on a formal grammar. The text gives few exact F1 values outside the synthetic and formal-language SpaDE results, and no base-model task-performance comparison establishing the performance cost of improved specialization.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted reconstruction error, per-concept sparsity, and other geometry or visualization results that do not directly measure latent specialization or co-occurrence. Also omitted figure-only details not explicitly described in the text.

untested.parts: Neurons of image classifiers are never examined. DINOv2 is analysed only through SAEs.
Neither the share of MLP neurons nor layer dependence is measured in language models.
Superposition is not tested as the cause of neuron polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization or noise is not tested as a source of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
No comparison of base-network activation functions or architectures on the share of polysemantic neurons, and no performance cost reported. Only SAE encoders vary.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Measurement dependence is not tested for neurons. Threshold and sparsity choices apply only to SAE latents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V5 labels are wrong. V5 concerns the activation function or architecture of the network whose neurons are polysemantic, not of an interpreter SAE trained on its activations. Many rows also compare the authors' own SpaDE method against baselines. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test whether individual neurons in image classifiers respond to unrelated inputs.
It studies SAE latents on a formal-language transformer, not the share of MLP neurons in language models responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
It does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than available neurons.
It does not test whether initialization, regularization, or training noise causes polysemanticity when there is enough capacity.

It compares SAE architectures and measures SAE-latent specialization, but does not compare the underlying networks' neuron polysemanticity, SoLU, or backbone architecture and regularization. It does not establish that changes in SAE-latent specialization come with no large loss in the underlying model's task performance.
It does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons with improved tools to establish that their unrelated inputs share a feature.

It varies SAE sparsity and reports F1 and co-occurrence, but does not test how inspecting different parts of an individual neuron's activation range or changing explanation-scoring methods changes its polysemanticity classification.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured concept-specific latent F1 scores on synthetic Gaussian clusters.

conditions.value: linearly separable and nonlinearly separable clusters

rows.measure: F1 score of most monosemantic latents
rows.value: F1 of 1 for the linearly separable concept; F1 for the nonlinearly separable concept bounded above by 0.5
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5 reports shaded region ±1SD for the top 5 latents
rows.note: The text attributes the lower F1 on the nonlinear concept to overlapping receptive fields with other concepts.
rows.check: Measures SAE latent F1 on synthetic 2D Gaussian clusters, not neurons of a trained network. Does not bear on V5's neuron-level claim.

rows.subject: SpaDE
rows.operation_detail: Measured concept-specific latent F1 scores on synthetic Gaussian clusters.

conditions.value: linearly separable and nonlinearly separable clusters

rows.measure: F1 score of most monosemantic latents
rows.value: Top F1 score of 1.0 for both concepts
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5 reports shaded region ±1SD for the top 5 latents
rows.note: The paper describes this as perfect precision and recall for the best-scoring latents.
rows.check: SAE latents on synthetic data. SpaDE is the study's own method, so this row compares its method with others.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-concept correlations among latent activations.
rows.note: The paper reports these correlations as evidence that the concepts are not clearly separated in the SAE latents.
rows.check: Co-occurrence of SAE latents, not polysemanticity of network neurons.

rows.subject: TopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-concept correlations among latent activations.
rows.value: Marginally lower correlations than ReLU and JumpReLU
rows.note: The paper describes TopK as doing marginally better, not as eliminating cross-concept correlation.

rows.subject: SpaDE
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-concept correlations among latent activations.
rows.value: No cross-correlations reported; spectral clustering identifies the concepts
rows.note: The paper also notes possible overspecialization into subclusters.
rows.check: SAE latents. This is the study's own method, and the text notes it may overspecialize.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured latent co-occurrence across concepts of different intrinsic dimensions.
rows.value: Correlations across concepts in the dense case; reduced in the sparse case
rows.note: The text says different concepts use different numbers of latents, but correlations remain in the dense setting.
rows.check: SAE latent co-occurrence on synthetic heterogeneous clusters, not network neurons.

rows.subject: TopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured latent allocation and co-occurrence across concepts of different intrinsic dimensions.
rows.value: Similar numbers of latents used across concepts; does not adapt allocation to concept dimension
rows.note: This reports the architecture-dependent specialization pattern described by the paper.
rows.check: Mislabelled: the measure is per-concept latent allocation, not co-occurrence. It concerns SAE latents, not network neurons.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic separability and heterogeneity experiments; formal-language and Imagenette SAE comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Specialization differs across SAE architectures: SpaDE reaches F1 1.0 on both synthetic concepts and on formal-language concepts, while the other architectures show lower or incomplete concept separation; reported latent correlations also differ by architecture (SYN-F1-RELU, SYN-F1-JUMP, SYN-F1-TOPK, SYN-F1-SPADE, SYN-COOCCUR-RELU, SYN-COOCCUR-JUMP, SYN-COOCCUR-TOPK, SYN-COOCCUR-SPADE, HET-COOCCUR-RELU, HET-COOCCUR-JUMP, HET-COOCCUR-TOPK, HET-COOCCUR-SPADE, LANG-F1-RELU, LANG-F1-JUMP, LANG-F1-SPADE, VISION-F1-SPADE, VISION-F1-RELU, VISION-F1-JUMP, VISION-F1-TOPK).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The reported synthetic, formal-language, and Imagenette SAE settings
reader_labels.reason: The outcomes are SAE-latent specialization, not the share of polysemantic neurons in the base networks, and no underlying-model task-performance comparison establishes the claimed low cost (all listed V5 rows).
